Nominal or real? Match the cash-price basis with the discount rate

Value one original inflation-adjusted spending schedule in two consistent ways, compare their equal present costs and inspect errors caused by mixing real cash with nominal rates.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Value one invented spending schedule using matching nominal and real conventions

Interactive planning lab

Equivalent annual real discount rate2.94%
Present cost using nominal cash and nominal discounting$171,117.36
Present cost using real cash and real discounting$171,117.36

Original deterministic valuation of one spending schedule. The base annual amount represents constant today-price purchasing power; future nominal payments increase at the selected general inflation assumption and occur at each year-end, starting one year from now. All rates are annual effective rates. Nominal here refers to money-price basis, not a quoted APR with a separate compounding frequency. The exact matching real rate is (1 + nominal rate) / (1 + inflation) − 1 and can be negative. Both consistent present-cost totals value the same payments on today’s comparison date and must not be added together. The intentionally mismatched calculations demonstrate convention errors; they are not alternative investment strategies. Inputs are assumptions, not observed inflation, available yields or recommended discount rates. No asset account, contributions, uncertainty, tax, fees, specific-category price changes, early payment, spending reduction or affordability assessment is modeled. Present cost is a valuation, not a promise that investing that sum will fund the schedule.

The central idea

Changing from future-price cash to today-price cash also changes the matching discount rate. With consistent dates and the exact conversion, both methods value the same payment schedule equally.

01

State what the dollars represent before entering a rate

A plan might express an expense as the cash that will be paid in a future year, or as the amount of today’s purchasing power that expense represents. Those are different descriptions of the same intended consumption. They require consistent treatment when calculating a present value.

This example specifies CAD 20,000 of annual spending in today’s purchasing power for ten years. The first payment occurs one year from now. Prices are assumed to rise by 2% every year, and the independently selected nominal discount rate is 5% annually.

All rates use annual effective compounding. “Nominal” here refers to a money-price basis that includes inflation. It does not mean a quoted annual percentage rate whose payment frequency or compounding convention still needs conversion.

The calculation values the schedule; it does not select an investment, simulate an account or establish a sufficient reserve. Every inflation and discount-rate input is hypothetical.

02

Translate the constant purchasing-power goal into future cash

At the chosen 2% price increase, the year-one payment is CAD 20,000 × 1.02, or CAD 20,400. The year-ten payment is CAD 20,000 × 1.02 to the tenth power, or approximately CAD 24,379.89.

The first chart places those growing nominal payments beside their constant today-price equivalent. It does not add them. Spending CAD 20,400 in year one is the assumed way to buy the consumption represented by CAD 20,000 today; it is not a second CAD 20,000 payment.

Across the ten dates, the nominal cash amounts total approximately CAD 223,374.31. The today-price amounts total CAD 200,000. Neither undiscounted total is the present value of the schedule at the selected rate.

This simple example assumes the relevant spending price rises exactly with its general inflation input. In practice, a particular category may change differently. Deflating a realistic schedule does not make those category differences disappear.

03

Convert the rate using growth factors rather than a rough subtraction

Write the nominal discount rate as n and inflation as i, both as fractions. The matching real discount rate r satisfies 1 + r = (1 + n) ÷ (1 + i).

With n = 0.05 and i = 0.02, the exact real rate is 1.05 ÷ 1.02 − 1, or approximately 2.941176%. Subtracting 2% from 5% produces 3%, which is a useful rough description at small rates but not the exact factor used here.

The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s explanation of real rates distinguishes that exact ratio from the subtraction approximation. The calculation below keeps the full derived rate so rounding does not create a false disagreement between methods.

A real rate can be negative when the selected inflation rate exceeds the nominal rate. That is allowed by this identity. It describes the assumed purchasing-power comparison; it does not establish an actual product return or a probability of preserving capital.

04

Discount the same economic payments on consistent bases

Under the nominal method, inflate each annual payment and then discount it with the nominal rate. Year t contributes CAD 20,000 × (1.02)t ÷ (1.05)t to present cost.

Under the real method, retain the CAD 20,000 today-price amount and discount it with the matching real rate. The contribution is CAD 20,000 ÷ (1.0294117647…)t. Substituting the exact rate identity makes this expression algebraically identical to the nominal one.

Adding the ten contributions gives approximately CAD 171,117.36 under either method. Both totals use today’s comparison date. They are alternative valuations of the same schedule and must not be added as separate funding requirements.

The paired bars deliberately show equal values for selected payment years. Their agreement is a calculation check, rather than two independent estimates supporting a forecast. ACCA’s inflation-appraisal explanation describes the corresponding cash-and-rate matching principle. This article applies it to original household-spending amounts without importing business-tax assumptions.

05

Measure the error when only one side of the convention changes

Suppose the cash is converted to its constant CAD 20,000 real amount, but the 5% nominal discount rate is retained. The resulting total is approximately CAD 154,434.70, which is CAD 16,682.66 below the consistent present cost.

The opposite mismatch keeps the growing nominal cash but discounts it at the lower 2.941176% real rate. That produces approximately CAD 190,213.73, or CAD 19,096.37 above the consistent total.

The signed bars compare those errors with zero. They do not represent investment gains, discounts negotiated on future invoices or additional cash flows. The underlying spending intention has not changed; the inconsistent valuation convention changed the answer.

At zero inflation, the nominal and real cash amounts coincide and the two discount rates coincide. Both mismatch errors then disappear. That boundary is a useful way to inspect the calculator without assuming that future inflation will actually be zero.

06

Change assumptions while preserving the consistency rule

The matrix varies inflation and the nominal discount rate, keeps the annual today-price spending and horizon selected, and derives the matching real rate in every cell. A larger future nominal bill raises its present cost when the nominal discount rate is held fixed.

If the nominal rate equals inflation, the derived real rate is zero. Each constant today-price payment then contributes its full CAD 20,000 to present cost. With ten payments, the consistent total is CAD 200,000, even though the future nominal payment amounts can be rising.

Dates matter independently of the price basis. This model starts at year one and uses year-end payments. An expense due immediately has no first-year discount, and monthly payments need their own timing convention. Changing dates while describing the result as the same schedule would change the comparison.

The matrix has no assigned probabilities, risk premium or current yield curve. Its cells are conditional arithmetic, not estimates of the likelihood of meeting a goal.

07

Keep a valuation separate from cash availability and investment risk

A present-cost figure does not make a future invoice smaller or ensure an account will earn the entered rate. It expresses a stream of payments on a common comparison date under selected assumptions.

Before turning that value into a funding plan, identify the available resources, their access dates, the actual investment or deposit terms and the consequences of a shortfall. An uncertain return used as a discount rate does not become guaranteed simply because the discounted total can be calculated precisely.

Use a consistent tax, fee and currency basis as well as a consistent inflation basis. This example calculates none of those adjustments. Its nominal and real methods agree because they describe the same cash schedule, dates and assumptions.

Record the annual spending definition, price assumption, payment timing and rate convention together. That record makes a future revision reviewable and helps prevent a switch in units from being mistaken for an improvement in the financial plan.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical figures use constant annual spending in today’s purchasing power, one inflation assumption and annual effective discount rates. They contain no observed inflation series, product yield, probability forecast or investment recommendation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
